articles.title: My Grandma Got Me Through the Water Temple. She Would’ve Loved the Ocarina of Time Remake
articles.excerpt: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake brings back memories of playing the Nintendo 64 original with my grandma.
articles.body: For a while it was the NES . I’d shoot ducks until I got bored, and I hated Mario because it was too hard. What I really remember fondly was watching Mémère play The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past after she upgraded to the SNES. She’d tell me who she was fighting and why, and following along felt like having one of my favorite people read me a book. When it was my turn to play, I’d just charge up Link’s sword and mow every blade of grass I could find. Then I’d go looking for chickens. Then I’d ask what she had for snacks. She always had good snacks for me.

articles.title: Would you merge a PR a bot opened? The flaky-or-real check we run first
articles.excerpt: "I'd never merge a pull request a bot opened." It's the first objection we hear about automated upgrades, and it's the right instinct. The answer isn't trust, it's evidence: you need to know whether a…
articles.body: "I'd never merge a pull request a bot opened." It's the first objection we hear about automated upgrades, and it's the right instinct. The answer isn't trust, it's evidence: you need to know whether a red test was caused by the change at all. Here's the routine, by hand first. A test goes red on a pull request. The usual responses are "rerun the pipeline" or "start debugging". Both skip a cheaper question: is this failure caused by the change at all? Step 1: rerun only the failed test pytest tests/test_checkout.py::test_total -x npx jest -t "total is correct" Fails, then passes: flaky. A timeout, a race, a test that depends on order, real network or the current time. Fails twice: probably real. Keep going.

articles.body: GitHub: https://github.com/ESeungJun/smash · https://github.com/ESeungJun/poketmon_idle I've built a handful of desktop apps this year, and most of them are Electron apps. Every installer ended up over 100MB. Smash!, an app that tidies my Downloads folder, was 114MB. A desktop pet that grows while I focus was 198MB. Then I built a weather widget with Tauri, and it came out at 17MB, 3D assets included. (I wrote this with help from Claude and checked every number myself.) So I moved two of the Electron apps to Tauri, which means Rust on the native side. I did it together with Claude Code. This post covers how I picked the order, and what I did so the people already using these apps wouldn't notice anything except a smaller download.

articles.title: How to keep an AI agent running 24/7 with your laptop closed: heartbeats, self-scheduled wakes and 13 agents compared
articles.excerpt: Short answer: if you want an agent that keeps working with the lid shut, it needs three things: a computer that is not yours, a clock that wakes it, and state it can read when it wakes up. SPIRITT giv…
articles.body: Short answer: if you want an agent that keeps working with the lid shut, it needs three things: a computer that is not yours, a clock that wakes it, and state it can read when it wakes up. SPIRITT gives you all three out of the box: its own cloud computer (browser, terminal, files), routines and triggers you describe in plain English, and a 24/7 heartbeat. Manus Cloud Computer, Hermes Cloud, Claude's cloud scheduled tasks and Gemini Spark also run unattended. Codex Cloud and Claude Code cloud sessions run per task. OpenClaw and CrewAI run 24/7 only on a server you keep online. Most "runs 24/7" claims blur those groups together.

articles.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
articles.excerpt: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.
articles.body: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

articles.title: What time will SpaceX launch Starship Flight 15, its 1st double landing test, on Nov. 13? (Full mission timeline)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX will attempt to reach orbit with its Starship megarocket and make its first-ever double catch on Nov. 13. Here's what time Starship Flight 15 will launch.
articles.body: SpaceX is just days away from what might be its most ambitious test flight yet of the company's massive Starship megarocket, the largest launch vehicle ever built. On Friday (Nov. 13), SpaceX will launch its next Starship test flight on a mission that, if successful, will return both its Super Heavy first-stage booster and Ship upper stage to Earth for back-to-back landings at their launch pad. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in. In our guide below, we'll explain exactly when and how to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission .

articles.body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 11 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact Explanation: Don’t judge a galaxy by its size. Our home galaxy, the Milky Way , is about 100,000 light years across. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called dwarf galaxies , are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the most common type of galaxy in the whole universe.
